label: HISTORY
title: Göbekli Tepe: Older Than Stonehenge by 6,000 Years. Who Built It?
description: Around 11,500 years ago, people who had not yet invented pottery raised carved stone pillars five metres tall on a hill in south-eastern Turkey. How was Göbekli Tepe found, how old is it really, and was it a temple or a village? Here is what archaeologists know, and what they are still debating.

sources.title: The Tepe Telegrams, German Archaeological Institute (DAI) Göbekli Tepe Research Project

lines.t: Jack, what came first: the temple or the village?
The village, surely. First farming, then villages, then temples. That's the order we learned at school.
What if I told you that people who had not even invented pottery raised carved stone pillars five metres tall?
When?
More than six thousand years before Stonehenge, and around seven thousand years before the pyramids of Giza.
You're talking about Göbekli Tepe.
I am. And the most fascinating part is that we still don't fully know who built it, or why.
Then let's start at the beginning. How was it found?
Göbekli Tepe lies near the village of Örencik in Şanlıurfa province, in south-eastern Turkey. It sits on a limestone plateau overlooking the Harran plain.
It is a mound about fifteen metres high. Its name means Potbelly Hill in Turkish, and a small shrine on the hill was visited by local people.
When did archaeologists first notice it?
In 1963, during a survey led by Halet Çambel of Istanbul University and Robert Braidwood of the University of Chicago. They collected thousands of flint tools on the surface.
But the true importance of the site wasn't recognised at the time.
So the stones waited another thirty years.
Exactly. In 1994, the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt, who had worked at a similar site called Nevalı Çori, re-examined the hill.
He realised that under the soil there was something monumental. Excavations began the following year, with the Şanlıurfa Museum and the German Archaeological Institute.
And what they found surprised everyone.
How old are these structures, exactly?
Radiocarbon dating shows the earliest structures were built between 9500 and 9000 BCE. That's roughly eleven and a half thousand years ago.
The site was expanded over the following centuries and used until at least 8000 BCE.
Let's put that in perspective. Stonehenge is about five thousand years old. The pyramids, about four and a half thousand.
Göbekli Tepe was built before writing, before the wheel, before metal, and even before pottery. That's why archaeologists call this period the Pre-Pottery Neolithic.
So these people were hunter-gatherers.
Largely, yes. The hill was surrounded by open grassland with wild wheat and barley, and herds of gazelle, wild sheep and wild donkeys.
How do we know the dates are right?
The first samples were confusing. Soil from inside the structures gave dates five hundred to a thousand years younger than expected.
So researchers dated organic material trapped in the plaster of the walls instead. That method confirmed the structures really were built very early.
What do these structures look like?
Picture large round or oval enclosures. Set into their walls are T-shaped limestone pillars.
In the centre of each enclosure stand two larger pillars facing each other. In Enclosure D, the central pillars are about five and a half metres tall.
Why the T shape?
The excavators believe the pillars represent people. Some have arms and hands carved along their sides, and belts and loincloths.
So the top of the T is the head, and the shaft is the body. Giant, stylised human figures.
What else is carved on them?
A whole bestiary. Snakes, foxes, wild boars, gazelles, wild sheep, ducks, scorpions, and especially vultures.
Different enclosures favour different animals. Snakes dominate in Enclosure A, foxes in Enclosure B. A later building even has lion reliefs.
All carved without metal tools.
With stone tools, in relief and engraving. Some floors were even made of burnt lime, hardened into a polished surface.
Göbekli Tepe is often called the world's first temple. Is that true?
That idea comes from Klaus Schmidt. He believed it was a ritual centre where hunter-gatherer groups from across the region gathered at certain times.
In his view, they met here, held great feasts, built together, and then scattered again.
Large numbers of butchered animal bones, gazelle, wild boar and deer, seemed to support this. Gazelles were only around seasonally, which suggests gatherings at particular times of year.
Schmidt even summed it up in a famous line: first came the temple, then the city.
That's a powerful idea.
It is. But findings published in 2019 changed the picture. Excavators found houses, extensive cereal processing, and tools of everyday life.
There are also cisterns cut into the bedrock that could collect at least one hundred and fifty cubic metres of rainwater.
So people actually lived here.
That's the newer interpretation. Today, researchers discuss Göbekli Tepe as a settlement that also had monumental buildings, not just a sanctuary for visiting nomads.
What the pillared enclosures were really used for is still not known for certain. That's the honest answer.

chapters.heading: How Many People Did It Take?

lines.t: Cutting, moving and raising pillars that heavy must have needed a lot of people.
Schmidt's team thought so. They estimated that at least five hundred people were needed to quarry the pillars, move them nearly half a kilometre, and build the enclosures.

But later experiments at the site gave a very different answer. They suggested that all of the later structures uncovered so far could have been built by twelve to twenty-four people in less than four months.
That's a huge difference.
And both are part of a genuine scientific debate. What is certain is that these people knew how to cut pillars from the bedrock and set them upright.
The buildings were often damaged by landslides, then repaired or rebuilt. Enclosure D was eventually filled with rubble by one of those slides.
So it wasn't built once and forgotten.
No. Over centuries, walls were added, spaces were changed, and some enclosures were made smaller. It was a place that was lived in and reshaped for a very long time.
Is Göbekli Tepe unique?
For a long time it seemed to be. But after detailed work at nearby Karahan Tepe in 2019, it became clear there are many similar sites in the region.
In 2021 this group of sites was named Taş Tepeler, the Stone Hills. Nevalı Çori, Hamzan Tepe and Sefer Tepe are among the places with the same kind of pillars.
How much of Göbekli Tepe has been excavated?
As of 2021, only about ten percent. Geophysical surveys suggest there are at least twenty large enclosures inside the mound.
In 2018 it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognised as one of the first manifestations of human-made monumental architecture.
Klaus Schmidt died in 2014. Excavations continue as a joint project of Istanbul University, the Şanlıurfa Museum and the German Archaeological Institute, led by the Turkish prehistorian Necmi Karul.
And it has become a major destination.
In 2024, about seven hundred and nine thousand people visited the site.
So, eleven and a half thousand years ago, people without pottery carved and raised five-metre stones.
And we have only seen a small part of the hill. More than twenty enclosures are still waiting under the soil.
To me the real question is: why did they build them?
What do you think? A temple, a gathering place, or the heart of a village? Tell us in the comments.
